paragraphs.text: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia type III (FHH3) is a disorder of extracellular calcium homeostasis. It is marked by elevated serum calcium and reduced urinary calcium excretion. Nesbit et al. (2013) noted that FHH1 and FHH2 usually have normal PTH levels, whereas FHH3 is characterized by increased serum PTH concentrations, hypophosphatemia, and osteomalacia. FHH is genetically heterogeneous: FHH1 maps to 3q21.1, FHH2 to 19p, and FHH3 to 19q13 (Nesbit et al., 2010).

paragraphs.text: McMurtry et al. (1992) described a large kindred with familial benign hypercalcemia. Of 46 members studied across 5 generations (ages 1.5 to 91 years), 19 were affected. In the 15 hypercalcemic subjects examined biochemically, serum immunoreactive PTH was measured in 3 separate immunoassays. Levels rose to supranormal values by about age 30 years and appeared to increase further after that. Serum alkaline phosphatase and creatinine were normal, but inorganic phosphate was lower than in unaffected kindred members. Of 5 affected adults older than 40 years who were studied radiographically, 3 had changes suggestive of osteomalacia. In a 51-year-old affected woman, iliac crest biopsy after tetracycline labeling confirmed defective skeletal mineralization. The authors suggested that the disorder may not be totally benign and that osteomalacia, perhaps due to mild hypophosphatemia, can develop in adulthood.

paragraphs.text: Hannan et al. (2010) performed linkage analysis in 34 informative members of the Oklahoma kindred, 19 of them affected, using 17 microsatellite markers and 7 SNPs. They confirmed linkage to chromosome 19q13, with a peak 2-point lod score of 6.92 at theta = 0 for D19S606. Recombinants in 3 individuals refined the locus to a 4.1-Mb interval (less than 10 cM) flanked by D19S112 and rs245111. This interval contained 135 protein-coding genes and 24 predicted genes. The authors also examined the region of mouse chromosome 7 that is syntenic to the interval. It contains 4 Casr-related sequences (Gprc2a-rs genes), but BLAST analysis found no human or primate homologs. The human syntenic region (22.0 Mb) and the mouse region (39.3 Mb) shared 2 conserved segments, which were inverted in man. An 11.6-Mb mouse region containing 35 genes, including the 4 Gprc2a-rs genes, was absent from the human genome. The authors concluded that FHH3 cannot be attributed to Gprc2a-rs abnormalities.

paragraphs.text: Nesbit et al. (2013) performed exome sequencing on 1 affected individual from each of 2 unrelated FHH3 kindreds, one from Oklahoma and one from Northern Ireland. Within the 3.46-Mb FHH3 interval on 19q13.3, the 2 patients shared only 1 variant: a C-T transition in exon 2 of the AP2S1 gene, predicting an arg15-to-cys (R15C) substitution. Sanger sequencing confirmed the variant. Restriction enzyme analysis showed that it cosegregated with the disorder in members from 4 generations of the 2 kindreds. The authors then sequenced AP2S1 in 50 unrelated FHH patients (23 males and 27 females) in whom CASR mutations had been excluded. They found 11 heterozygous missense mutations, all affecting arg15: 4 were R15C, 3 were R15H, and 4 were R15L. They concluded that AP2S1 arg15 mutations may cause FHH in more than 20% of patients without CASR mutations. In functional studies, all 3 mutations decreased the sensitivity of CaSR-expressing cells to extracellular calcium (see PATHOGENESIS).

paragraphs.text: Nesbit et al. (2013) performed exome sequencing on affected individuals from 2 unrelated FHH3 kindreds, one from Oklahoma and one from Northern Ireland. They identified a heterozygous C-T transition in exon 2 of the AP2S1 gene, predicting an arg15-to-cys (R15C) substitution. Sanger sequencing confirmed the variant, and restriction enzyme analysis showed that it cosegregated with the disorder in members from 4 generations of the 2 kindreds. The authors found the R15C mutation in 4 further unrelated FHH patients among 50 who were negative for CASR mutations. In HEK293 cells stably expressing CaSR, the R15C mutant raised the EC50 for extracellular calcium above that of both wild type and vector alone, suggesting a possible dominant-negative effect. Cells with the mutant also showed reduced CaSR endocytosis after stimulation with extracellular calcium.
